Detectors.NET

8 minutes read

.NET

The dotnet detector reports .NET release lines that no longer receive fixes, in the SDK a repository pins and in the target frameworks of its projects, and direct NuGet dependencies their publisher has deprecated. It reads global.json, project files, Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props, and packages.lock.json. It is stable (decision 0013): it is scored on the public corpus and held to the 0.95 precision floor, and a change to one of its rule ids, finding ids, or documented declaration forms is listed in the changelog. It is part of the documented product contract. The reasoning for the detector is in Decision 0012.

What it reads

File Declaration
global.json sdk.version
*.csproj, *.fsproj, *.vbproj, Directory.Build.props TargetFramework and TargetFrameworks (a semicolon list, one declaration per entry) in a PropertyGroup
*.csproj, *.fsproj, *.vbproj PackageReference items, with the version from the Version attribute or a <Version> child
Directory.Packages.props PackageVersion items (central package management)
packages.lock.json the resolved version of each "type": "Direct" dependency
*.cs using directives and calls of deprecated packages, to list the files a migration touches

It walks the repository up to eight directories deep (at most 500 matching files) and does not follow symbolic links. It skips .git, node_modules, vendor, dist, build, bin, obj, target, .venv, venv, fixtures, __fixtures__, and testdata. The dotnet CLI is never run and MSBuild is never evaluated.

What it reports

  • An SDK pin or a target framework on a release line that is past its end of support under the .NET support policy, at high severity. An SDK X.Y.Z belongs to the line X.Y, so 3.1.426 is the 3.1 line. netcoreapp3.1, net5.0, and net6.0-windows are read as the lines 3.1, 5.0, and 6.0. The rules cover 1.0, 1.1, 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, 3.0, 3.1, 5.0, 6.0, and 7.0 today; .NET Core 3.0 and older are named ".NET Core X.Y" in the findings.
  • A line whose end Microsoft has announced but that has not happened yet (.NET 8 and 9, 2026-11-10) as a scheduled-end-of-life finding at low severity, so a severity gate set to high does not fail on a date that is still ahead. When the date has passed, a reviewed change turns the rule into the end-of-support rule with the same id (decision 0010).
  • A direct PackageReference or PackageVersion on a NuGet package whose publisher deprecated every version as legacy, at medium severity. The registry has four such rules today: WindowsAzure.Storage and Microsoft.Azure.Storage.Blob (replaced by the Azure.Storage.* packages), Microsoft.Azure.DocumentDB (replaced by Microsoft.Azure.Cosmos), and Microsoft.Azure.ServiceBus (replaced by Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus).
  • A Direct entry in packages.lock.json, only for a rule that names specific versions. A package deprecated at every version is reported once, where it is declared.
  • For the package rule, the .cs files that import or call it, with an impact summary.

Each finding carries its rule's source, replacement, migration steps, and verification commands (dotnet build && dotnet test).

What it intentionally does not judge

  • netstandard2.0 and netstandard2.1 are API specifications, not runtimes, and have no end of life. They are ignored.
  • .NET Framework targets (net48, net472, ...) follow the Windows lifecycle, not the .NET policy. They are listed as unclassified; see Decisions for the forms outside the project files.
  • An MSBuild property ($(TargetFramework), Version="$(Ver)"), a floating version (1.*), and a version range ([1.0,2.0)) cannot be decided without evaluating MSBuild. They are listed as unclassified with their file and line, never guessed.
  • Anything under an element or group with a Condition, and anything set through <Import> or inherited from a file Offing is not looking at, is skipped.
  • A PackageReference with no version is unclassified, unless central package management (ManagePackageVersionsCentrally set to true) is enabled in its directory or above, where the version is judged in Directory.Packages.props.
  • A global.json without sdk.version, a version that is not a number, and a version under msbuild-sdks (which belongs to a build SDK package, not to .NET) pin no SDK.
  • Malformed or oversized files (over 1 MiB) produce nothing, not partial results. A global.json may contain comments but not a trailing comma.
  • A dotnet-version given to actions/setup-dotnet and a mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/* base image in a Dockerfile name a runtime too, but this detector does not read workflows or Dockerfiles. A dotnet-version is judged by the GitHub Actions detector and the base images by the container detector, both with the rules of this one (decided in #845 and #846).

Decisions for the forms outside the project files

#827 listed the .NET forms that got no verdict. Each one is now either judged or recorded as out of scope, with the reason:

Form Decision Reason
.NET Framework targets (net48, net472, v4.x in TargetFrameworkVersion) Out of scope. Still listed as unclassified. Framework is supported as part of Windows, so each version follows the lifecycle of the Windows releases it ships with, not the .NET release policy that every rule here cites. A rule needs an authoritative Microsoft lifecycle source per version and a statement of which Windows releases it assumes; the releases index the dotnet-1 importer reads has no Framework data. Judging it from the .NET policy would be a guess. A future decision may add a Framework rule set with its own source.
MSBuild properties, <Import> chains, and Conditions Out of scope. Properties are unclassified; imported and conditional values are skipped. A target set in an imported file or a property needs MSBuild evaluation: resolving the import graph, property functions, and conditions. Offing parses repository files and never evaluates them or runs dotnet, so a verdict would be a guess. A repository can put the target where it is read: a literal TargetFramework in the project, or a global.json pin.
dotnet-version of actions/setup-dotnet Judged, by the github-actions detector with this detector's rules. The version lives in a workflow, which this detector does not read. See the GitHub Actions detector (#845).
mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/* base images Judged, by the container detector with this detector's rules. The tag lives in a Dockerfile or Compose file. See Container base images (#846).

Known limits and false-positive boundaries

  • A target framework is a statement about what the project builds for. A library can multi-target an old line on purpose; Offing reports the declaration and cannot know the intent. A global.json SDK pin names the toolchain that builds the repository, which is closer to the truth.
  • A sample, test, or tool project in a repository that still targets an old line is reported like any other project.
  • Source usage is found for .cs files only. using directives, aliases, global using, a type reached by its full name, and a type reached by its simple name when its own namespace is imported are found. Verbatim strings (@"…", $@"…"), including ones that end in a backslash, contain doubled quotes, or span lines, are masked correctly, so code after them is still read. Three cases are deliberate limits, because attributing them would need type or symbol resolution that a text scan cannot do without guessing:
    • A method called on an instance (account.CreateCloudBlobClient()) is not found. The receiver's type is declared elsewhere (a field, a parameter, var), and matching on the method name alone would report unrelated types that share it. The file is still listed if it has the using directive.
    • using static N.Type; is reported as an import but binds no name. A bare Parse() may be a member of the enclosing class, which C# prefers over the imported one, so it is not attributed.
    • F# (*.fs) and Visual Basic (*.vb) sources are not read. Their import and call syntax differs from C#, and the project files that declare the packages are read regardless.

Data

The rules are in registry/dotnet.json and ship in the data bundle. The importers dotnet-1 (the official releases index) and dotnet-2 (NuGet deprecation metadata for a reviewed list of packages) draft new rules for review; see Lifecycle importers.

Validation

Eighteen public repositories at pinned commits are in the corpus, scored by every detector. Six were chosen knowing their result (selection: "targeted"): four that targeted a past-support line or depended on a deprecated package until their maintainers moved on (Sloth, Sharp.BlobStorage, sourcelink, machinery), one whose test projects target .NET 8 and so carry the scheduled low-severity finding (xunit.analyzers), and one with no findings (LibreAutomate, which targets net10.0-windows). Twelve were chosen by a rule fixed before Offing ran on them (selection: "blind"), described in Validation. Eight of them have no finding because they target .NET Framework or netstandard, which this detector does not judge. Four have findings: Ceras (netcoreapp2.1 and 2.2, which had no rule until this change, so the first scan of it missed them), DlibDotNet (netcoreapp2.0, 2.1, and 3.1), Chrome-Developer-Mode-Extension-Warning-Patcher (net6.0), and SharpSocks (net5.0 and net6.0).

Across the eighteen repositories there are 84 expected dotnet findings, all matched. For the twelve blind repositories, the target frameworks, SDK pins, and package references were listed by hand and compared with the report: every judged form was reported and nothing else was (the 50 findings in DlibDotNet are 46 netcoreapp2.0, two netcoreapp2.1, and two netcoreapp3.1 declarations, counted independently of Offing). Recall is therefore measured on the forms in "What it reads" only; the unjudged forms listed above are outside it, and the blind sample shows they matter: two of the twelve repositories name a runtime in a workflow or Dockerfile that is not read. The counts, selection, and precision floor are the evidence behind the stable level in benchmarks/thresholds.json. Corpus-wide evidence already meets every stable count in decision 0013 (repositories with findings, expected findings, zero-finding repositories, and blind share), including .NET findings reported through workflow and container declarations that reuse these rules.
